title: Marketing Fundamentals
summary: Learn the marketing mix, segmentation and positioning, market research, pricing and break-even, digital promotion with acquisition costs, and branding, loyalty and ethical marketing, with worked numbers.
audience: Entrepreneurs, business students, sales staff and anyone promoting a product or cause

body.p: Marketing is the work of understanding what customers need and creating, communicating and delivering value that meets those needs profitably. It is much more than advertising: it shapes which products a business makes, what they cost, where they are sold and how people hear about them.

list: Product: what you sell, including quality, design, packaging, brand and after-sales service.
Price: what customers pay, including discounts and payment options.
Place: how the product reaches customers: shops, markets, agents, delivery and online.
Promotion: how you communicate: advertising, social media, word of mouth, sales promotions and public relations.

body.p: Services add three more Ps: people (staff who deliver the service), process (how it is delivered) and physical evidence (the setting and materials customers see). A hair salon's skill, booking process and clean shop all shape the customer's experience.

body.tip: Start from the customer's problem, not your product. People do not buy a drill; they buy a hole in the wall.

body.p: No product suits everyone. Segmentation divides a market into groups with similar needs; targeting chooses which groups to serve; positioning decides how you want those customers to see you compared with competitors.

list: Demographic: age, income, gender, family size, occupation.
Geographic: region, city or rural area, climate.
Psychographic: lifestyle, values, interests.
Behavioural: how often they buy, what benefits they seek, brand loyalty.

body.p: Estimate before you invest. If a city has 2 000 000 households, about 30% are likely buyers of a water filter, and each spends R500 a year on filters and refills, the yearly market is 2 000 000 x 0.30 x 500 = R300 million. Your realistic share will be a small part of that at first.
A clear positioning statement helps: "For busy parents in Lagos who want healthy lunches, our meal boxes are the most convenient option because we deliver to school by 11 a.m."

body.tip: A segment worth targeting must be big enough, reachable through channels you can afford, and willing to pay.

body.p: Research reduces guesswork. Secondary research uses existing data such as industry reports, government statistics and competitors' websites. Primary research collects new data: surveys, interviews, observation and test sales.

steps: Recognise a need (my phone is too slow).
Compare alternatives on price, quality, brand and convenience.
Buy, influenced by the shopping experience and payment options.
Evaluate after buying; satisfied customers return and recommend.

list: Cheap tests beat long debates: sell a small batch at a market stall or run a small online ad before scaling.
Track why people do not buy, not just why they do.
Watch competitors: their prices, promotions and reviews show gaps you can fill.

body.tip: Ask customers about what they did, not what they would do. "How much did you spend on lunch last week?" is more reliable than "Would you buy our lunch?"

body.p: Price is the only P that brings money in; the others cost money. Common methods:

list: Cost-plus: add a markup to cost. A product costing R40 with a 50% markup sells for R60. The profit margin on the selling price is 20 / 60, about 33.3% (markup and margin are different).
Competitor-based: price near similar products, then justify any premium.
Value-based: price according to the value the customer receives, often the most profitable approach for unique products.
Penetration pricing: start low to win share quickly; skimming: start high and lower over time.

body.p: Break-even units = fixed costs / (price - variable cost per unit). With monthly fixed costs of R12 000, price R60 and variable cost R40, each sale contributes R20, so the business must sell 12 000 / 20 = 600 units a month to break even. Every unit beyond that adds R20 profit.

body.tip: Small price rises often add more profit than big sales drives. Test a modest increase on a part of your market before deciding.

body.p: Promotion moves people from not knowing you to buying and recommending. A simple funnel describes it: awareness, interest, consideration, purchase and loyalty.

list: Word of mouth and referrals, still the most trusted.
Social media: content, short videos, community groups and paid ads targeted by location and interest.
Messaging apps for orders and updates, with customers' consent.
Search: appearing when people search for what you sell, through good websites and business listings.
Radio, outdoor and print, still powerful in many markets.
In-store promotion, sampling and events.

body.p: If an online campaign brings 10 000 visitors and 2% buy, that is 200 sales. If the campaign cost R20 000, the customer acquisition cost (CAC) is 20 000 / 200 = R100. Compare this with what a customer is worth: a customer who spends R50 a time at a 40% margin, twice a month for 6 months, brings 50 x 0.4 x 2 x 6 = R240 of gross profit, 2.4 times the CAC, a healthy ratio.

body.tip: Track every campaign with a unique code, link or phone number so you know which ones actually produce sales.

body.p: A brand is the set of ideas and feelings people have about a business: its name, logo, voice, quality and the experiences they have had. Strong brands earn trust, allow better prices and survive mistakes.

list: Deliver what you promise, consistently.
Make it easy to buy and easy to complain; fix problems quickly and generously.
Reward repeat customers through loyalty schemes, personal service or early access.
Collect feedback and show customers what changed because of it.
Keeping customers usually costs less than finding new ones.

body.p: Claims must be truthful and supported; consumer-protection laws prohibit misleading advertising, hidden fees and unfair terms. Respect privacy when collecting customer data, and get consent before sending marketing messages, as data-protection laws such as POPIA and the Nigeria Data Protection Act require. Be especially careful when marketing to children.

body.tip: Ask, "Would I be comfortable if this advert or message appeared on the news?" If not, change it.
